title: Pumping and co-transport in a gut lining cell
caption: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to push 3 Na⁺ out into the blood for every 2 K⁺ it brings in, keeping sodium low inside the cell. Sodium then flows in from the gut through SGLT1 and drags glucose with it, against the glucose gradient: secondary active transport. Glucose leaves for the blood down its gradient through GLUT2.
alt: A gut lining cell between the gut lumen above and the blood below. On the gut side, sodium ions and glucose enter together through a co-transporter. On the blood side, a sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in using ATP, and glucose leaves through a carrier protein.
description: Gut side: Na⁺ flows in from 140 to 12 mmol per dm³, down its gradient, through the SGLT1 co-transporter.
Glucose enters through the same protein from 0.5 to 8 mmol per dm³, against its own gradient: the sodium gradient pays for it.
Blood side: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out (12 to 145) and 2 K⁺ in (4 to 140), both against their gradients.
Each cycle of the pump carries one more positive charge out than in, so the inside of the cell is left negative.
Glucose leaves for the blood (8 to 5) by facilitated diffusion through GLUT2.
Concentrations are illustrative: SGLT1 goes on absorbing glucose even when the gut holds less than the cell.
